title: Noun phrases
summary: Use articles, quantity words and countable or uncountable nouns accurately.

sections.title: Can you count it?
content: Try saying ‘two apples’ and then ‘two rices’. The first sounds right because you can count apples. You usually do not count rice in this way.
This matters because it decides which small words you can put before a noun.

sections.title: Ask two questions about the noun
content: Can I count it? Countable nouns take a or an when there is one, and they can be plural. Uncountable nouns such as water, advice and information have no plural. Use much and a little with them, and many and a few with countable nouns.
Has the reader already met it? Use a or an when you first mention something. Use the when the reader already knows which one you mean.
Choose a or an by sound, not spelling: a university, an hour.

sections.title: Work through a short example
content: Take: ‘Dani found ___ wallet near the gate. ___ wallet had no name inside.’ The first wallet is new to the reader, so a fits. The reader now knows which wallet, so the second gap needs The.
Take: ‘We did not get ___ advice from the guide.’ Advice cannot be counted, so much fits and many does not.

sections.title: Say what the noun is first
content: Before you choose, say whether the noun can be counted and whether the reader already knows it.

sections.title: Choose without the label
content: Read the whole sentence, because the clue may come after the gap. Then read it again with your choice in place.

sections.title: Find where it went wrong
content: Count error: I treated an uncountable noun as countable. First-mention error: I used the for something new, or a for something the reader already knew. Sound error: I chose a or an by spelling.
Reading error: I missed a clue later in the sentence.

sections.title: Try a new text
content: Complete one unseen short text with three gaps. If you need a hint or get it wrong, you will try a new text with different nouns.
